evidence_quotes.quote: Yarilena receives water from the Tod-Ceduna supply system, which also services other towns across Eyre Peninsula.
Yarilina has 15 houses but is charged as if it were a single household thus it quickly exceeds the limit of 125 KL and is charged at the higher rate.
The community is responsible for maintaining and covering the costs associated with the extensive internal infrastructure.
The average daily per capita domestic water use obtained from data collected over a 20-month period is 209 L/d.
Comparing the mains metre reading with that of the sum of the household metre readings for the same period indicated that leaks accounted for up to a 57 percent discrepancy.

The household roof capacity to harvest more rain, together with the accumulating water debts being paid for out of the community’s boating business, prompted them, with the help of the research team, to apply for an additional rainwater tank for each house through a Commonwealth Community Water Grant in 2006.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines community and household domestic water supply access, utility billing, rainwater harvesting, and internal reticulation infrastructure in Yarilena, a remote Aboriginal homeland community of 15 houses (57 residents) in South Australia.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies Criterion 2 under BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study examines the National Water Initiative (NWI) Agreement, utility governance, and Indigenous community governance. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it directly examines tariff and cost-recovery rules (NWI Clause 66(v) full cost recovery vs Community Service Obligation; SA Water's tiered tariff structure combined with bulk-billing a 15-house community at a single boundary meter as if it were one household so consumption above 125 kL is charged at US$1.03/kL, alongside an internal US$5/week rent deduction) and utility regulatory/responsibility boundary rules (SA Water's service responsibility ending at the property-boundary meter, leaving the community financially responsible for 5 km of internal piping and high-pressure burst leaks, plus a proposed provider transfer to the District Council of Ceduna).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical case-study evidence from Yarilena (part of a multi-community study of Aboriginal communities in South Australia), including 20-month domestic water consumption monitoring (209 L/capita/day), a comparison of boundary mains meter readings against summed household meter readings (identifying up to a 57% leak discrepancy), household rainwater storage inventories, and utility billing/expenditure records.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports outcomes directly relevant to domestic water quantity/consumption (209 L/capita/day), infrastructure reliability and water loss (burst internal pipes from mains pressure causing up to a 57% meter discrepancy and isolation of 1.5 km of piping to a remote house), and affordability/cost burden (higher-tier bulk water charges and accumulating community water debts paid from the community's boating business).
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (Yarilena Aboriginal community in South Australia; community and household levels, 15 houses, 57 residents), rule-type exposure (NWI cost-recovery rules, SA Water single-household bulk boundary metering under tiered pricing, and property-boundary maintenance liability), outcome (per capita water consumption, 57% leakage discrepancy, accumulating water debts), and study design (empirical case study with 20-month meter monitoring and policy/institutional analysis) are all identifiable.

study_design: Empirical single-community case study (embedded in a multi-community study) combining 20-month domestic and boundary water meter monitoring, expenditure/billing analysis, and qualitative institutional/policy analysis
population_and_sample: Yarilena remote Aboriginal homeland community west of Ceduna, South Australia (community and household levels: 15 houses, 57 residents)
exposure: National Water Initiative (NWI) cost-recovery and mainstream service-delivery rules, SA Water tiered pricing with single-household bulk metering at the property boundary (billing 15 houses as one household above 125 kL and assigning liability for 5 km of internal piping to the community), and internal community levy ($5/week rent deduction) and grant-funded rainwater harvesting
outcome: Domestic water consumption (209 L/capita/day over 20 months), mains-to-household meter leakage discrepancy from high-pressure pipe bursts (up to 57%), household/community water costs and accumulating water debts, and rainwater harvesting storage/cost savings (5%)
rationale: Included. While the first half of the article discusses Australia's National Water Initiative (NWI) and Noel Pearson's welfare-reform framework, pages 421-423 present an empirical case study of domestic water service access in the Yarilena Aboriginal community (15 houses, 57 residents) drawing on 20 months of water consumption data, boundary-versus-household meter comparisons, and billing records. It directly examines rule-type tariff, metering, and utility-boundary mechanisms under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 readings—specifically SA Water billing all 15 houses as a single household at the property-boundary meter under a tiered tariff (pushing community usage above 125 kL into the higher US$1.03/kL tier) and ending utility responsibility at the property boundary (leaving the community financially liable for 5 km of internal piping, high-pressure pipe bursts causing a 57% leak discrepancy, and accumulating water debts)—alongside community governance and rainwater-harvesting responses. Confidence is medium because methodological details of the underlying research project are reported concisely within a short journal article, though all eligibility criteria (c1-c6) are satisfied.
